items.title: Price discrimination can be welfare-enhancing
items.claim: A monopolist charges different prices to different consumer groups for the same product. Is this always bad for welfare?

options.text: Not necessarily. Price discrimination can increase output (more consumers served) and total welfare, even when redistributing surplus from consumers to firms. Whether it's welfare-positive depends on demand elasticities and whether output expands

items.reveal:
Pigou's 1920 classification: first-degree (perfect, individual reservation prices); second-degree (volume or quality discounts, e.g. Kindle Unlimited tiers); third-degree (group-based, e.g. student/senior pricing, geographic).

Schmalensee (1981) and Varian (1985) showed welfare effects depend on whether discrimination raises total output. Airlines, pharmaceuticals (Ramsey pricing across countries) and education (income-based fee remission) all use price discrimination. Personalisation through data raises new concerns about welfare and fairness.
items.why: Microeconomic textbook intuitions about welfare often need conditioning on output effects. Price discrimination is a clean example of where the textbook needs caveats.

items.title: FDI flows have plateaued since 2015
items.claim: Global Foreign Direct Investment flows reached record highs in the 2000s. UNCTAD data from 2020 onwards shows what pattern?

options.text: FDI flows have plateaued and partially fragmented along geopolitical lines (US-EU vs China-aligned blocs); 'slowbalisation' or 'fracturing globalisation' is the now-common framing
All FDI is now in the metaverse

items.reveal:
UNCTAD World Investment Report data: global FDI peaked at $2 trillion in 2015; 2022 flows were $1.3 trillion. Trade as a share of global GDP also flattened.

Drivers: US-China trade tensions (tariffs from 2018), COVID supply-chain reshoring, geopolitical fragmentation (Russia-Ukraine, Taiwan strait), reshoring/nearshoring policies (US CHIPS Act, EU Chips Act, IRA).

The 'end of history' globalisation narrative of the 1990s-2000s has been substantially complicated.
items.why: Globalisation is not a one-way ratchet. The political economy of trade and investment has shifted in ways that affect macroeconomic forecasting and corporate strategy.

items.title: The Bank of England became independent in 1997
items.claim: Gordon Brown announced operational independence for the Bank of England in May 1997, days after Labour's election victory. What's the standard rationale?

options.text: To allow politicians to set interest rates directly

To insulate monetary policy from short-term political pressure, given evidence that independent central banks (Bundesbank, Fed) had lower average inflation. The Treasury sets the target; the Bank sets rates

items.reveal:
Alesina and Summers (1993) had documented the inverse correlation between central bank independence and inflation across OECD countries. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 1989 Act pioneered explicit inflation targeting.

UK target: 2% CPI from 2003 (RPIX 2.5% before). The MPC has 9 members, votes monthly. Brown's surprise announcement preceded the post-1997 inflation stability period.

Independence has been challenged in some quarters since 2010s rate decisions; the Bank's bond buying in autumn 2022 (LDI crisis) raised questions about coordination with Treasury.
items.why: Institutional design — who decides what, accountable to whom — is as much a part of macroeconomic policy as the decisions themselves.
